topic: Why smart teams agree their way into bad decisions: groupthink, how it starts in ordinary meetings, and simple habits that break it
scope_note: Conservative sheet for a 2.5 minute corporate soft-skills lesson. The core is Janis's description of groupthink and the remedies he proposed, plus a few well-known related ideas (pluralistic ignorance, Asch's conformity studies, the premortem, independent views before discussion). No percentages, effect sizes or counts are claimed anywhere. Janis's model is treated as a useful description with mixed evidence, not a tested law, and the lesson must say so plainly. Named sources sit in reference_hint for the reviewer; the lesson need not name them. The story team in the lesson is invented and carries no facts.

facts.statement: The psychologist Irving Janis developed groupthink into a theory of how close-knit groups of capable people make poor decisions.
facts.reference_hint: Janis, Victims of Groupthink (1972); revised as Groupthink (1982)

facts.statement: The word groupthink was in use before Janis: the journalist William H. Whyte used it in a Fortune magazine article in 1952.
facts.caveat: If the lesson says where the term comes from, the safe wording is that Janis developed or popularised it, not that he invented the word.

facts.statement: Janis described groupthink as a way of thinking in which a close-knit group's drive for agreement overrides a realistic look at the alternatives.
Janis's point was that the cause is the wish to keep agreement, not a lack of intelligence: his cases involved experienced, capable decision makers.
One of the case studies Janis used was the failed Bay of Pigs invasion, planned by advisers to US President Kennedy in 1961.
facts.reference_hint: Janis (1972), chapter on the Bay of Pigs
facts.caveat: That Janis used the case is established; how well groupthink explains it is debated by historians. The brief allows at most a one-line mention.

facts.statement: Among the warning signs Janis described are self-censorship, where members keep their doubts to themselves, and an illusion of unanimity, where silence is taken as agreement.
Janis also described direct pressure on anyone who disagrees, and members who shield the group from information that challenges the plan.
A leader who makes their preferred option known early is one of the conditions Janis linked to groupthink, and later studies found groups with such directive leaders discussed fewer alternatives.
facts.reference_hint: Janis (1982), lack of impartial leadership; Leana (1985), Journal of Management; Esser (1998) review
facts.caveat: Supported in several studies, but from small and mostly laboratory or historical samples. Say 'tends to' or 'can', never 'always'.

facts.statement: When each person privately doubts something but assumes everyone else accepts it, a group can go along with a view few of its members actually hold; psychologists call this pluralistic ignorance.
facts.reference_hint: Katz and Allport (1931); Prentice and Miller (1993), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
facts.caveat: A general social psychology idea, not part of Janis's model itself; the lesson may describe it without naming it.

facts.statement: In Solomon Asch's conformity experiments, many people went along with a group's clearly wrong answer on a simple judgement, and conformity dropped sharply when just one other person gave the right answer.
facts.caveat: A laboratory task with strangers, not a work meeting; results vary across later replications, cultures and eras. Quote no percentages.

facts.statement: Janis recommended that a leader stay impartial at the start, holding back their own preference, so that others feel free to raise alternatives.
facts.caveat: A recommended practice, not a tested guarantee.

facts.statement: Janis recommended giving at least one member the job of critical evaluator, or devil's advocate, so that objections are expected rather than risky.
facts.reference_hint: Janis (1982), remedies; Nemeth and colleagues (2001), European Journal of Social Psychology
facts.caveat: Research by Charlan Nemeth found a role-played objection can be discounted and does less than genuine dissent. Present the role as a way to make real doubts easier to say, not as a fix on its own.

facts.statement: Janis also suggested inviting outsiders to challenge the plan, and holding a second-chance meeting to air remaining doubts before the final commitment.
Asking each person to write down their own view before open discussion keeps their judgements independent and reduces the pull of whoever speaks first.
facts.reference_hint: Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), on decorrelating errors in meetings; Delbecq and Van de Ven, nominal group technique
facts.caveat: Widely recommended practice with supporting research on independence of judgement; not a guarantee.

facts.statement: A premortem asks a team to imagine the plan has already failed and to write down why, before the decision is final, which makes raising doubts part of the task.
facts.reference_hint: Gary Klein, 'Performing a Project Premortem', Harvard Business Review (2007)
facts.caveat: A widely used practice; the lesson must not attach a measured improvement to it.

facts.statement: Research on speaking up at work finds people often stay quiet about concerns because they expect raising them to be pointless or to cost them socially.
facts.reference_hint: Morrison and Milliken (2000), Academy of Management Review; Morrison (2014), Annual Review of Organizational Psychology
facts.caveat: Describes common reasons, not a single cause; no prevalence figure is claimed.

facts.statement: The evidence for Janis's full model is mixed: later studies support some parts, such as the effect of a directive leader, more than others, and many researchers treat groupthink as a useful description rather than a proven law.
facts.reference_hint: Esser (1998), Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes; Turner and Pratkanis (1998); Baron (2005)
facts.caveat: The lesson must carry this in one plain line where the model is introduced.

not_claimed: Any percentage or count of decisions, meetings or projects ruined by groupthink.
Asch's conformity rates as numbers (for example 'a third' or 'three in four people conformed'); the direction only.
That Janis coined the word groupthink (Whyte used it first; Janis developed the theory).
That groupthink is the proven cause of a specific disaster such as Challenger or a named corporate failure; those are interpretations.
That close-knit or friendly teams are the problem, or that cohesion alone causes groupthink; the evidence for cohesion is weak.
That smart or expert people are more prone to groupthink than others.
That a devil's advocate, a premortem or any single habit guarantees a good decision.
That diverse teams are immune to groupthink.
That group brainstorming produces more or better ideas than people working alone first.
